messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol had been driving home from the hospital after a long day in her architecture office when her phone rang with the call that fractured the rest of her life. Her younger brother had been struck down suddenly and was in the emergency department, and by the time she arrived the antiseptic smell hit her first, sharp and clinging, before she even found the ward. She remembered standing in a corridor full of incomprehensible chatter, voices overlapping in English and a language she could not make out, and feeling more disoriented by that blur of sound than by the bright lights or the white walls. The hospital had felt enormous and airless, all corridors and doors and bad news. She was in a place designed to save lives, yet what she carried out of it was the image of her brother failing despite everyone’s urgency. In the months that followed, any physical location that resembled that place — a clinic lobby, a parking garage, even certain stretches of polished hallway in office buildings — could pull her straight back into that night, with her body bracing before her mind had fully caught up. Once Marisol had concluded that the world was not safe and that she could not trust her own steadiness, those reminders seemed to multiply; she began taking the longer route past the medical district and leaving any situation that felt too similar before the fear could build.

At first Marisol told herself she was simply tired. But the triggers had a way of altering the whole day. A whiff of antiseptic in a pharmacy or the hospital smell on a relative’s coat would leave her nauseated and hollowed out; when conversations around her turned into a jumble of voices she could not parse, she became tense and irritable, convinced something was about to go wrong. Because those cues hit her so hard, Marisol started arranging her days around avoiding them entirely, taking the longer route past the medical district, declining dinners near the hospital, and leaving clinic waiting rooms before she had to sit with the smell and the noise. Those moments did more than frighten her. They hardened into meanings she could not shake: she had lost faith in people, in life, and in any higher power that might have been listening that night. Once Marisol had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that she could not trust her own steadiness, almost anything could confirm it — a whiff of antiseptic, the wrong tone of voice in a corridor, or a jumble of overlapping voices — and those reminders drove her to cross streets, change routes, and leave places before the fear could build. Because she was certain that danger could surface without warning, ordinary sights and sounds started to snag her attention more easily, and a passing disinfectant smell or a burst of overlapping voices could feel like proof that something bad was about to happen again. She began to feel as though others could see what happened to her just by looking at her, as if the shock were written across her face and in the way she held herself. Even at work, reviewing plans with clients in her glass-walled office, she caught herself imagining they could tell she was altered, damaged, no longer the composed architect she had been. The world around her had become charged with reminders, and each reminder seemed to confirm that the life she had built no longer carried the same meaning.

To keep from being overwhelmed, Marisol started arranging her days around what she could not bear. She avoided seeing friends, letting texts sit unanswered and declining dinners she once enjoyed. She also avoided medical cues with unusual determination: she would not step into hospitals unless there was no other choice, refused ambulance rides she felt she “should” have been able to tolerate, and even postponed physical examinations when work made it easy to explain them away. When she did have to pass a clinic, she would cross the street or take the longer route, but those detours left her feeling ashamed and smaller, as if she were confirming her own suspicion that she could not face what life demanded. The more she withdrew, the more she came to feel that nothing in her life was meaningful anymore. That emptiness did not stay abstract for long. Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the clinic she would not enter, the corridor she no longer crossed, the dinners she stopped attending — and the map of her life began to fill with absences that kept the event in view. She began to push herself to exercise excessively, turning long runs and punishing gym sessions into a way of forcing her body into order, as if fatigue might crowd out the memories and prove she was still in control. Yet the harder she trained, the more depleted and isolated she felt, and the less inclined she was to reconnect with friends or with the parts of her work that had once felt creative. In that depleted state, a walk past the medical district on her way back from the office, or the sight of an ambulance outside a client site, could provoke the same tightness and dread that sent her retreating again.

Marisol’s efforts to outrun the feeling did not restore confidence; they deepened her belief that something essential had been taken from her and that she had become visible in her brokenness. Her exercise, meant to keep her from falling apart, left her exhausted and more certain that she was no longer the person others remembered, which made social contact feel even harder and the hospital corridor even more dreaded if she happened to pass one. She noticed that the more she avoided friends and medical settings, the more unfamiliar ordinary life felt, and the more meaning drained from the days that were already organized around warning signs. In the office she could still draft elegant buildings and speak fluently about materials, but afterward she would sit alone at her desk, staring at the plans, feeling that the work belonged to someone else. What finally brought her to seek help was a recent visit to an outpatient clinic for a routine issue, when the smell of disinfectant and the sound of staff talking over one another in clipped, overlapping phrases left her shaky enough that she had to leave before being seen. She came in now because she was frightened that she would keep shrinking her life around these reactions, and because beneath the anger and exhaustion she was still hoping that some part of her could learn to live in a world that had not stopped being meaningful.
